Issued at 438 AM CDT Mon Jul 27 2026

An amplified upper level ridge persists from the Southern 
Rockies through the Northern High Plains early this morning, 
while a surface ridge extends from Saskatchewan into western 
North Dakota. The upper ridge is forecast to remain nearly 
stationary through today, although a mid level shortwave 
currently located between Yellowstone and the Great Salt Lake 
will eject towards the Black Hills later today. This will induce
lee troughing from the Black Hills into southwest North Dakota 
while the surface ridge slides eastward into central North 
Dakota. With all this occurring underneath the right entrance 
region of an upper jet streak, enough forcing should be present 
to initiate storms along the higher terrain of northeast 
Wyoming/southeast Montana this afternoon, with east-
northeastward propagation. A consensus of CAMs clips the 
southwest corner of the state with this activity between mid 
afternoon and early evening. Forecast confidence is high in 
effective bulk shear around 35-40 kts, but there is greater 
uncertainty in buoyancy. CAPE could first be regulated by the 
degree of moisture advection between the lee trough and 
downstream surface ridge, then by the strength of boundary layer
mixing. Ensemble averaged CAPE is generally no greater than 
1000 J/kg, and a lingering warm nose aloft could keep convection
elevated. The main hazard with any storm entering far southwest
North Dakota later today is wind gusts, possibly as strong as 
60 mph. The SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook does clip far southwest
North Dakota with a Conditional Intensity Group level 1 for 
damaging winds as high as 75 mph, but given the location and 
footprint of the pool of buoyancy, think significant winds are 
much more likely to be confined south of the stateline. Outside 
of far southwest North Dakota, some CAMs have been simulating a 
variety of shower or thunderstorm activity in other parts of the
state throughout the day. But with forecast cloud bases closer 
to 15 kft, not expecting anything beyond just a few sprinkles at
the surface, with most of what develops being virga. 

Today will be a few to several degrees cooler for most 
locations. The projected thickness of smoke aloft introduces 
uncertainty into the high temperature forecast for today. Given 
observed conditions both overhead and upstream last evening, and
little to no change in HRRR modeled vertically-integrated smoke
concentrations from then through this evening, our high 
temperature forecast for today is just slightly cooler than the 
NBM, with mid and upper 80s far north to mid 90s southwest and 
south central. Near-surface smoke concentrations are also 
projected to be similar to what arrived yesterday, so reduced 
visibility cannot be ruled out. The mention of smoke in the 
forecast has been extended through tonight.

The upper level ridge is projected to more or less remain in 
place through Wednesday. The forecast for Tuesday is similar to 
that for today, with slightly warmer high temperatures around 90
to 100, lingering smoke both at the surface and aloft, and low 
probabilities (less than 20 percent) for isolated afternoon and 
evening thunderstorms across southern North Dakota. Synoptic 
scale forcing looks very weak on Tuesday, so any convection that
does initiate would likely be on account of convective 
temperatures being breached. Slightly higher CAPE is forecast on
Tuesday with deep layer shear around 30 kts, so a stronger 
storm cannot be ruled out. On Wednesday, the thermal ridge axis 
is forecast to pivot into North Dakota ahead of stronger 
shortwave energy ejecting from the Great Basin. Widespread high 
temperatures and maximum heat indices around 100 are in the 
forecast for Wednesday. Convection could initiate near a lee 
surface trough along the ND/MT border Wednesday afternoon, and 
should become more widespread in western North Dakota with the 
arrival of the shortwave Wednesday evening, spreading into 
central North Dakota overnight. Forecast confidence in both CAPE
and shear remains low, but a Marginal Risk was introduced to 
western North Dakota for the Day 3 Convective Outlook, and CSU 
machine learning guidance also highlights low severe storm 
probabilities on Wednesday.

The eastward progression of the shortwave could be slow enough 
to keep showers and thunderstorms in central and eastern North 
Dakota on Thursday. After a slight cool down to highs in the mid
80s to mid 90s for Thursday and Friday as a result of the 
downstream shortwave digging into the Great Lakes and Ohio River
Valley, the upper level ridge is forecast to rebound and become
even more amplified from the Desert Southwest to the Canadian 
Prairie this weekend. Ensemble guidance projects the thermal 
ridge axis to be over the Northern High Plains on Sunday, which 
once again has medium chances for temperatures exceeding 100 
degrees. A major pattern shift could finally be on the way
